# Branch protection

The rules are in `branching.mdc`; this file is what enforces them.

Guarded in-repo first, so a bad merge never leaves the machine:

- `.githooks/pre-push` — refuses to push `main` unless its new tip has the **same tree** as `dev`
  (or `origin/dev`). A genuine `dev → main` merge leaves main's tree identical to dev's; a direct
  commit on `main`, or a merge of any other branch, moves the tree away and the push is blocked.
  Run `bash scripts/install-git-hooks.sh` once per clone. Bypass in a real emergency with
  `git push --no-verify`.
  It also runs `npm run check` (the harness's own checks, then each stack pack's) once per push when the
  pushed range touches anything beyond docs-only paths and `package.json` defines `check`, so CI
  confirms rather than discovers. A project whose suite is too heavy for every push leaves
  `check` out. It always checks `.claude/rules` and `AGENTS.md` against the `.mdc` files, and, when
  the range touches `docs/plans/`, the plan tables against `plans.mdc` (a docs push to `dev` runs no CI).
- **Agent hooks** (`.claude/settings.json`, `.cursor/hooks.json` → `scripts/command-guard-hook.mjs` → `scripts/command-guard.mjs`):
  `core.mdc` → Guard rails, plus the project's own rules (below).

Backed by GitHub rulesets server-side, where `--no-verify` cannot reach:

- **`main: production`** — no deletion, no force-push, PR required, all required checks green. No bypass.
- **`dev: no force-push or deletion`** — no bypass.
- **`dev: PR and checks`** — PR plus required checks, admin-bypassable so a wedged CI cannot lock the repo.

Required checks are matched by **name**. Renaming a CI job — or adding a required one — without
updating the ruleset leaves a check that never reports, and every PR blocks forever. Change both
together. Skipping a required job via `if:` still reports (skipped counts as passing); skipping
the *workflow* (`paths-ignore`, `[skip ci]`) reports nothing and bricks the PR.
The template's `.github/workflows/ci.yml` requires **`Checks`** and **`Build`**, plus
**`Only dev merges to main`** (`guard-main-source.yml`) on the `main` ruleset. `Change scope` is
not required. A stack pack whose CI job must gate merges names it in its `pack.json` →
`requiredChecks` (`pnpm stack:list` shows the pack; the pack's own rule names the job):
`bootstrap-repo.sh` adds each present pack's to both PR rulesets, and `pnpm stack:remove <pack>`
prints the ruleset edit to make, since the job goes with the pack and a required check nothing
reports blocks every PR. Bootstrap only creates rulesets that don't exist yet, so adopting a pack
later means adding its `requiredChecks` to both PR rulesets by hand (Settings → Rules).
A project whose CI differs lists its own required names in
`branch-protection.project.mdc`. `scripts/bootstrap-repo.sh` creates all three rulesets.
Rulesets need a public repo or a paid plan; without them the pre-push hook and the red check
are the only stops.

## Project guard rules

The guard is harness, so a project never edits it. Its own rules go in `command-guard.project.json`
at the repo root (project-owned, optional). A stack pack ships its rules as
`scripts/command-guard.d/<pack>.json` (harness-owned; `deny` and `ask` only). Same JSON for both:

```json
{
  "deny": [{ "match": "^make\\s+deploy\\b", "reason": "Deploys go through CI." }],
  "ask": [{ "match": "^npm\\s+publish\\b", "reason": "Publishing is the user's call." }],
  "allow": [{ "command": "dropdb app_test", "reason": "The throwaway test database." }]
}
```

- **Matching.** Rules see each command the way the built-in rules do: split like a shell splits
  it, through chains and `bash -c`. `match` is a regex (`"flags": "i"` is the only flag) read from
  the program that runs, after `VAR=x`, `env`, `sudo`, `pnpm` and friends; anchor it with `^`.
  Optional `unless` reads the whole command from its first word, prefixes kept, with each
  `VAR=` at its last assignment (the one the shell uses). So it can require an inline loopback
  `DATABASE_URL=…`. `unless` can't see `.env` or the shell's exports; the built-in database rules
  read both, and `pnpm <script>` through to its command.
- **Exemptions are narrow.** An `allow` entry is one plain command, compared word for word; only
  quotes and spacing may differ. No ``$ ` & ; | < > ( ) { } [ ] * ? ~``. It lifts only a
  data-delete deny of exactly that command: the built-in delete list or a pack's deny. Anything
  more stays refused: a prefix, flag, redirect, or extra argument. An exemption that would meet
  any other built-in rule (branch protection, Ready, merges, reruns, `--no-verify`, destructive
  SQL, migration tools) makes the file broken. The project's own deny and every ask still win. Packs can't exempt.
- **Agents don't write their own way out.** The hook doesn't see the edit tools, so an agent never
  adds an exemption or edits a rule file to get a refused command through (`core.mdc`). Exemptions
  are the user's call, in a reviewed PR. A shell write to the guard's own files (`sed -i`, `rm`,
  `mv`, `chmod`, a redirect into `scripts/command-guard*.mjs`, a rule file, or the hook config) asks.
- **Order.** Deny beats ask beats exemption. With no verdict, Claude Code's own permissions
  decide. Cursor's hook must always answer, so there no verdict goes out as `allow`.
- **Failure is loud.** An absent file changes nothing. A file that is present but broken makes
  the guard refuse every shell command and name the file and the error. Broken means bad JSON, an
  unknown key, a missing reason, a key given twice in one object, or a pattern that doesn't
  compile. The agent stops and tells the user, who fixes the file or sets `WHIPPLETREE_GUARD=off`.
  A timed-out hook lets the command run, so the guard never runs into the host's timeout (10 s).
  It fails closed to **ask**, never to allow: a command line over its size budget (64k characters)
  or a read over its time budget (250 ms) asks, and an exception in the guard asks and names the
  error, so a guard bug reaches the user instead of letting the command through unseen. Behind
  that budget sits a watchdog (3 s, `WATCHDOG_MS`): the hook's whole evaluation runs under it,
  and past it the guard stops mid-run and asks, naming the watchdog. That covers what the budget
  can't, such as a rule pattern that backtracks badly (still keep patterns simple: each one costs
  the user a prompt). A blocked system call can't be stopped, so each one bounds itself: a branch
  lookup gives up after 1 s (a FIFO or a slow repo) and asks, and a rule file that
  isn't a regular file counts as broken. All of that needs the guard to load: the hooks run
  `scripts/command-guard-hook.mjs`, which blocks every command (exit 2, the reason on stderr) when
  the guard doesn't parse or isn't there, or exits any other way than with an answer, since Claude
  Code runs a command whose hook exits 1. Hook input with no command in it asks.

## Self-hosted runners

Learned running a Mac mini and a Linux laptop as runners. A self-hosted job bills no Actions minutes.

- **Switch:** set the repo variable `LINUX_RUNNER` to the machine's labels as JSON
  (`["self-hosted","Linux","thinkpad"]`). Checks and Build move; Change scope stays hosted. To roll
  back when the machine is offline and required checks stall, delete the variable.
- **Machine prerequisites:** the runner is non-admin, so no `apt-get`/`sudo` in a job. System
  libraries a job needs are installed by hand, and so is any toolchain a present pack's CI step
  takes from the runner image instead of installing (each pack's rule says which, and at what
  version). Docker (runner user in the `docker` group) for
  service containers; that group is root-equivalent, fine for a solo private repo.
- **No cache on self-hosted.** `actions/cache` restores a hosted runner's cache to the wrong path
  and still reports a hit; the persistent machine keeps its own store (`setup-node-pnpm` skips it).
- **Machine-wide resources** (a fixed port, a service container on a host port, a lock file) go on
  a label carried by exactly one runner instance, e.g. `e2e`. Extra instances without it
  parallelise the rest.
- **Wall-clock:** one instance runs jobs one after another (a web + iOS project: ~15 min per full run versus 6–7
  hosted). Add instances before blaming the machine.
